2.4.m: Sūta said: / When they had gone to Goloka, the Vaiṣṇava realm beyond darkness, / Śivaśarman, of great wisdom, spoke words to the youngest son.
The Brāhmaṇa said: / "O Somaśarman of great wisdom, you are intent on devotion to your father; / protect the great jar of nectar given by me now.
I shall go on a pilgrimage to sacred fords with this wife [of mine]." / [Somaśarman said:] "So be it, O fortunate one, I shall guard it well."
Having placed the jar in the hand of that noble-minded, wise [son], / he performed uninterrupted austerity for the duration of ten years.
The righteous-minded [son] guarded the jar day and night, unwearied. / Then that illustrious Śivaśarman returned,
having created an illusion, of great wisdom, together with his wife, to [test] that son. / Having become afflicted with leprosy, and his wife likewise,
the two of them, made by illusion, appeared like lumps of flesh. / To the presence of that dreadful twice-born Somaśarman
the two arrived. Seeing them utterly distressed on all sides, / the illustrious Somaśarman was overcome with supreme compassion.
Bowing to their feet, his neck bent with devotion, [he said]: / "I see none like you endowed with austerity
and with hosts of auspicious virtues; what is this that has happened to you? / Like servants, all the deities ever attend upon you,
receiving your command, O best of the twice-born, drawn by your splendor. / By what sin has this painful disease arisen in your body,
O best of Brāhmaṇas? Tell me the reason for that! / This virtuous mother is exceedingly meritorious, devoted to her husband;
she who by her husband's grace can create the three worlds— / how can she suffer distress? Is there no fruit of austerity?
She who, casting off passion and hatred, through various deeds / serves her beloved like a god, devoted to her elder—
how can she suffer distress, [afflicted by] the very painful leprosy?" / Śivaśarman said: "Do not grieve, O fortunate one; the fruit born of action is experienced
by a human being who is bound to action consisting of sin and merit. / Perform the cleansing of both of us afflicted with disease,
and the nursing, O fortunate one, if you desire merit here!" / When this auspicious speech was spoken, the illustrious Somaśarman [said]:
"I will certainly perform the service of you two endowed with merit! / By me, a sinful, wicked, wretched person, O best of the twice-born,
what is to be done here this very day, who did not worship his guru?" / Having spoken thus in distress, grieved by their suffering,
he cleaned away the phlegm, urine, and feces of them both; / he washed their feet and massaged their limbs.
Filled with devotion, he himself also [prepared] their bathing places and the like; / for to that illustrious Brahmin Somaśarman, these two were his highest gurus.
Placing them upon his shoulders, that best of men, righteous in nature, carried them to holy waters; / and having bathed both with his own hands with auspicious [rites],
with excellent mantras, knowing the Veda, and according to the rules of bathing, / as well as offering libations to the ancestors and worship to the deities,
that righteous one continually had both perform [the rituals]; / he himself made offerings into the fire and cooked unsurpassed food.
Greatly pleased, he satisfied these two great gurus; / and on bed and seat, that Brahmin continually put them to sleep.
He constantly provided both with all necessities such as garments and flowers; / and he would offer both betel rich in numerous fragrances.
The highly fortunate Somaśarman also fulfilled their needs; / he continuously gave [them] roots, milk, and excellent food.
Whatever both desired, the illustrious Somaśarman constantly [provided]; / by this systematic course of service, he always gladdened them.
The truly righteous Somaśarman served his parents reverently; / yet calling Somaśarman, his father, harsh [in nature], would revile him.
With harsh, reproachful words he would strike him in the presence of sages; / even when the task had been performed and the meritorious deed done, he would repeatedly say to his son:
‘You have done nothing good for me, you disgracer of the family!’ / In this way, with diverse words, harsh and painful,
Śivaśarman, ever afflicted, struck him with blows of a staff. / Even when treated thus, the righteous [son] never became angry.
Through thought, speech, and threefold deed, / he, ever contented, served his father.
In the same manner did Somaśarman day by day [serve] his mother. / Realising this, Śivaśarman reflected upon his own conduct:
‘Nectar was brought for my sake by Viṣṇuśarman; / endowed with merit, he is righteous and devoted to his father at all times.
When a long time, numbering hundreds [of days/years], had passed in this manner, / his father, Śivaśarman, seeing his devotion, reflected:
“Formerly I said to my noble son named Yajña: / ‘Son, scatter these pieces of your mother here and there!’
My word was kept by him; no pity was shown to his mother. / That was a lesser pain to one intending to strike what was lifeless.
Indeed, a daring act was done by the son Vedaśarman; / yet I consider this [son's conduct] greater, since he does not waver,
even if made to endure a rash deed for merely a moment. / Moreover, he is endowed with truth and the power of ascetic practice;
even in constant worship, greater [virtue] is seen in him. / Therefore, an examination of his ascetic practice was made at the right time.
Through devotional disposition and truth, the son does not falter at all; / even though by illusion leprosy was shown on my own limbs,
he feels no disgust at phlegm, urine, and feces; / and with his own hands, the illustrious one cleanses the sores daily.
The wise one provides foot massages and cleaning; / he constantly endures my unbearable and terrible speech.
Even when scolded and struck, he ever speaks pleasing words. / Thus, enduring sorrow, my son is of great intellect.
I deem him an ocean of sorrows, yet afflicted by many afflictions; / I shall remove his sorrow by the grace of Viṣṇu.”
Having reflected in his mind, the wise Brahmin Śivaśarman / then performed an illusion again, and the liquid was removed from the jar.
Then, summoning Somaśarman, he said: / ‘The nectar that destroys disease was placed by me into your hands.
Give it to me quickly so that I may drink it, / whereby I may become free from disease today through the grace of Viṣṇuśarman.’
When these words were thus spoken by the sage Śivaśarman, / Somaśarman, rising up in haste, [went to] the water pot.
Then, seeing it empty and devoid of nectar, [he thought]: / ‘By what sin's doing, by whom has this unpleasing thing been done to me?’
Having thus become full of anxiety, Somaśarman was exceedingly sorrowful: / "When shall I recount the events before my father?"
"Then my guru, afflicted with disease, will become angry." / Having reflected for a very long time, the highly intelligent Somaśarman [resolved]:
"If truth resides in me, if [I have performed] service to my guru, / [and] if austerity was formerly performed by me with an honest heart,
and if righteousness was truly maintained through self-control, purity, and the like, / then let this jar become filled with nectar—there is no doubt."
As soon as the fortunate one, having thus reflected, looked, / the jar immediately became filled with nectar once again.
Seeing that, the illustrious Somaśarman, filled with joy, / approached his guru, bowed down, took the jar quickly, [and said]:
"Take, O father, this jar of milk that has arrived; / drink, O fortunate one, and be free from illness without delay."
Hearing this most auspicious statement, sweet in syllable, / conveying truth and righteousness from his son,
Śivaśarman, overwhelmed with great joy, spoke these words:

2.5.m: Śivaśarman said: / "By your austerity, self-control, purity, and service to your guru, / and by your devotion and right disposition, I am pleased with you today, O good son.
I cast off this deformed appearance; receive happiness from me." / Having spoken thus to his son, the brāhmaṇa revealed that [divine] form.
He saw his two gurus just as they had stood previously: / both radiant, noble-minded, resembling the disk of the sun.
He bowed with true devotion at the feet of both noble ones; / then, having taken leave of his son, filled with great joy,
that righteous, best of men, together with his wife, through the grace of Viṣṇu / and through his own merits and the practice of yoga, attained Keśava.
That sage entered the Vaiṣṇava abode, the station difficult to obtain; / for the station that grants liberation is not attained by other merits and austerities.
Only through meditation on Viṣṇu, ritual placements, contemplation, knowledge, and hymns of praise / is Madhusūdana seen—not through gifts or pilgrimages.
By the yoga of absorption and knowledge the supreme station is seen, / just as the brāhmaṇa, through great yogas, entered the Vaiṣṇava body.
Sūta said: / Then the splendid Somaśarman performed austerity there; / he regarded gold and ornaments as equal to a stone or a clod of earth.
With diet conquered, that righteous man was devoid of sleep; / having abandoned all sense-objects, he resorted to solitude.
Seated in a yogic posture, free from longing, without possessions, / the exact hour of the time of death then arrived for him.
Dānavas arrived near the brāhmaṇa Somaśarman, / when the hour of death had arrived, as his life-breaths were about to depart,
in the great sacred site of Śāligrāma, which increases the honor of the sages. / Some Daityas cried out, and some Dānavas cried out;
such a great noise then entered the ear-cavity / of that very best of brāhmaṇas, Somaśarman, after a long time.
While fixed in contemplation of knowledge, fear born of the Daityas entered him; / by that very contemplation, indeed out of fear of the Daityas at that time,
the life-breaths of that noble soul quickly departed; / filled with fear of the Daityas, he indeed came under the power of death.
Therefore, he was born in the house of a Daitya as the son of Hiraṇyakaśipu; / in the great battle between gods and Asuras, he was slain by the disc-wielder.
Even while fighting, by that great-souled Prahlāda / the state of Vāsudeva endowed with the universal form was clearly seen.
Through his previous practice of yoga, knowledge arose in that noble one; / he remembered all the former deeds of Śivaśarman.
"Formerly I was named Somaśarman; I have entered a Dānava body. / When from this body shall I go to the pure, supreme, solitary abode,
"I shall go by means of great merits known as knowledge, which grant liberation." / By the great-souled Prahlāda, as he was dying in battle,
such thought was formerly made; hear, O best of the twice-born! / Thus was recounted that which destroys all doubt.
Sūta said: / When Prahlāda was slain in battle by the god of gods who bears the discus, / that Kamalā, loving, whose son was slain, wept.
She who was the mother of Prahlāda and beloved of Hiraṇyakaśipu / mourned day and night with immense grief for Prahlāda.
To his beloved, the devoted wife, highly fortunate, named Kamalā, / weeping day and night, Nārada said:
"Do not grieve, O fortunate one, for your son, O sharer in merit; / slain by Vāsudeva, your son will return.
"Again endowed with auspicious characteristics, your son shall be of great intellect; / and his name will once more be Prahlāda."
Devoid of demonic states and endowed with godhood, / revered by all the gods, he will rejoice in the sovereignty of Indra, O auspicious one.
Be happy, O fortunate one, forever with that son; / but this good news must not be disclosed by you, O lady, to anyone.
You should act as if unaware; always keep it well hidden." / Having spoken thus, the brāhmaṇa Nārada, best among sages, departed.
In the womb of Kamalā, there will be his incomparable rebirth; / and 'Prahlāda' will indeed be the name of that great-souled one, according to this narrative.
Having reached childhood, O brāhmaṇas, he contemplated Kṛṣṇa alone; / by the grace of Narasiṃha, he became the king of gods in heaven.
Having attained godhood and the matchless station of Indra, / he, whose self was knowledge, will go to liberation, the supreme abode of Viṣṇu.
Countless, O fortunate ones, are the manifold conditions of creation; / delusion should not thus be harbored by wise, noble persons.
All this has been recounted to you as asked, O best of the twice-born; / ask another question, O fortunate one, and I will shatter your doubt.
The victory of the gods and the great destruction of the Dānavas / was indeed brought about by the god of gods, and the three worlds were established.
The sages said: / "To whom did the status of Indra, who bears the name among the gods, belong? / By whom was it given? Tell us in detail, O best of the twice-born."
Sūta said: / "I shall declare in detail how that fortunate, best of men / attained the status of Indra through the most sacred merit.
When all those Daityas were slain in the great battle, / when the wicked ones were utterly destroyed by the noble Govinda,
then the gods, together with the Gandharvas, Nāgas, and Vidyādharas, / all addressed Mādhava with joined palms:
‘O Blessed One, Lord of the gods of gods, O Hṛṣīkeśa, reverence to You! / We make a request to You; let all of it be heard.
Make for us a ruler, protector, and righteous king, / of pure dharma, O Keśava, as Indra, governor of the world,
relying upon whom the people of the three worlds may obtain happiness, O God!’ / Vāsudeva said: ‘O fortunate ones, in My world, endowed with Vaiṣṇava luster,
the best of brāhmaṇas has dwelt for a long time; / the time for that noble-souled brāhmaṇa, who has been residing in My world
and is devoted to Me, has been completed, O best of gods; / through Vaiṣṇava luster, he will indeed be your protector.
He, righteous, will become the delighter in dharma; / he will be your protector and sustainer, that best of brāhmaṇas.
That righteous one will exist for the purpose of your protection, / as the son of Aditi, the noble-minded one named Suvrata.’
he will become of great strength and great heroism, and he shall be Indra.’ / Sūta said: Having thus granted excellent boons to the gods, the Lord of gods,
all the victorious gods, along with Viṣṇu, best of beings, / then went to see their father Kaśyapa and their mother.
Those great-souled ones bowed to both of them seated comfortably; / with folded hands and filled with great joy, they all said:
‘By the grace of you two, we have indeed attained godhood.’ / Overcome with great joy, he addressed the gods with these words.
Kaśyapa said: / ‘Indeed, you who always abide in truthful dharma, / by the grace of us two and by the power of ascetic practice,
have attained godhood and the imperishable state. / Filled with great affection, I grant a boon to these [gods]:
you shall be immortal, ageless, and imperishable, / having all desires fulfilled and endowed with all perfections.
By my grace, the gods, Nāgas, Gandharvas, and great Asuras [shall honor you].’ / Viṣṇu said: ‘Choose a boon, auspicious one, O glorious mother of the gods!
Whatever is desired in your mind, that I grant to you with certainty.’ / Aditi said: ‘Formerly I became a mother of sons by your grace, O Mādhava.
All these sons I obtained are immortal, ageless, imperishable, and fond of virtue; / listen, O Madhusūdana!
Above all, you, O Govinda, granter of the fulfilment of all desires, / should dwell in my womb and become my son.
So that I may constantly rejoice with you as my son, O Keśava, / fulfill this great, noble wish, O Lord!’
Vāsudeva said: / ‘For the purpose of divine work, you must assume a human form; / then I shall certainly take up residence in your womb.
When the twelfth yuga arrives, to remove the burden of the earth, / I, the son of Jamadagni, the best of Brahmins named Rāma,
endowed with valor and fiery energy, and for the destruction of all Kṣatriyas, / shall become your son, foremost of all wielders of weapons.
When the twenty-seventh yuga, called Tretā, arrives, / I shall become your son named Rāma, O faithful wife!
Listen, O virtuous one: I will again become your son / when the twenty-eighth yuga arrives at the end of Dvāpara.
For the destruction of all Daityas and the removal of the earth's burden, / I shall without doubt become your son named Vāsudeva.
Now, O auspicious lady, carry out my righteous command: / give birth to a handsome son endowed with all auspicious marks,
accompanied by true dharma, all-knowing, and granting everything, O goddess; / I shall grant him Indra-hood, and he too will become Indra.’
Hearing this speech, filled with immense joy [she thought]: / ‘By the grace of the God of gods, my son will become Indra.’
‘So be it, O illustrious Lord, I shall carry out your word.’ / Then all those deities went indeed to their own abode.
Together with Hari, all of them were free from anxiety and filled with joy. / Sūta said: Having reached her fertile season, the wise Aditi spoke to Kaśyapa.
"Lord, grant a son who will enjoy the position of the ruler of the gods." / Having thought for a moment, the brahmin spoke to that resolute woman:
"So be it, blessed woman; you shall have a son. / He will be the creator of the three worlds, and indeed the enjoyer of sacrifices."
Having placed his hand upon her head, the best of brahmins, / radiant and endowed with true dharma, performed ascetic penance.
A radiant being named Suvrata used to dwell forever in Viṣṇu's realm; / when his merit was exhausted, O best of brahmins, from Viṣṇu's realm,
his descent [took place] by the power of karma, O best of brahmins; / that ascetic entered the holy womb of Aditi, O brahmins.
In order to enjoy the status of Indra through his true and meritorious action, / that goddess carried the embryo by virtue of holy ascetic penance.
Free of indolence, having gone to live in the forest, the virtuous woman performed ascetic penance; / a hundred divine years passed as the mother of the gods engaged in ascetic penance.
As she performed severe ascetic penance, difficult even for gods and asuras to perform, / she became endowed with splendor by virtue of that penance and fiery energy,
resembling the brilliance of the sun, like a second sun itself; / blazing, she shone as she entered the highest meditation.
She attained an increase in beauty by the fiery energy of her ascetic penance; / devoted to asceticism and meditation, feeding on air, that female ascetic
Dakṣa's daughter then shone exceedingly. / The siddhas and all the ṛṣis, as well as the gods of great might,
praised that fortunate lady and protected her with great devotion. / When her hundred years were complete, Viṣṇu arrived there.
He spoke to the blessed Aditi, who was endowed with ascetic penance: / "Goddess, the embryo is fully mature; the time of childbirth has arrived.
Nourished by your very ascetic penance and augmented by your brilliance, / release, release this embryo this very day, renowned lady!"
Having addressed her thus, the lord of gods went to his own abode. / When the momentous time arrived, the goddess gave birth to a son.
[She bore] a son endowed with luster, like a second sun, / handsome, with charming limbs all over, endowed with all auspicious marks,
four-armed, large-bodied, a world protector, lord of the gods, / covered with blazing flames of energy, bearing a discus and a lotus in his hands,
with a face resembling the orb of the moon, highly intelligent, / shining, immensely wise, endowed with the fiery energy of Viṣṇu,
adorned with other divine marks and divine states, / complete with all auspicious characteristics, moon-faced and lotus-eyed.
The three gods arrived, as did the ṛṣis who had crossed to the end of the Vedas, / the gandharvas, then the nāgas, the siddhas, and likewise the vidyādharas.
The seven divine ṛṣis of ancient and supreme might, / and other holy sages who bestow auspicious merit,
those great-souled ones arrived, their minds overflowing with joy, / when that fortunate, glorious lord was born.
All the deities arrived, as well as the ascetic mountains, / all the oceans beginning with the ocean of milk, and pure rivers likewise.
Then all moving and unmoving beings became delighted; / with auspicious rites, all the lords of gods held a great celebration.
Troupes of apsarases danced, and the gandharvas sang charming songs; / then the gods and the brahmins, masters of the Vedas, with Vedic mantras
praised that great-souled son of Kaśyapa. / Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra, as well as the Vedas, came together,
accompanied by their limbs and secondary limbs, when that mighty one was born. / Whatever beings endowed with merit exist in the three worlds, O best of men,
all assembled right there when that mighty one was born; / with sacred songs and great celebrations, they performed auspicious rites.
All, overflowing with joy and possessing great might, worshiped [him]. / The three gods beginning with Brahmā, along with Kaśyapa and Bṛhaspati,
performed the naming rites for that great soul: / "Famous as Vasudatta, he is also your son Vasuda;
his name is Ākhaṇḍala, and again your name is Marutvat; / you are Maghavan, Biḍaujas, and also Pākaśāsana;
and your son is celebrated as Śakra and indeed Indra." / These were the names given to that great soul
by all the deities, who were pleased and joyful in their minds. / The great divinity caused the bath and the rites of passage to be performed.
Summoning Viśvakarman, they presented ornaments; / they gave those holy, divine [ornaments] to that great soul.
When that fortunate one, the king of gods, was born as a great soul, / all the deities of great might then experienced such joy.
On an auspicious lunar day, under a favorable lunar mansion, at an auspicious hour, by the great-souled [gods], / he was established in the state of Indra and consecrated with most auspicious rites.
The rank of Indra was attained by him through the grace of that wielder of the discus. / The radiant Vasudatta, lord of the gods, performed ascetic penance,
endowed with fierce brilliance, armed with thunderbolt, noose, and goad.
Sūta said: / Observing the fierce power of all his penance, Śukra recited a verse: / "Who else in the worlds will ever become like him, so wondrous to behold?
By the grace of Viṣṇu, there is no greater soul; divine sovereignty has been attained by him in this very world.
There will be no other equal to him in the worlds, whose power is fierce from ascetic penance."

2.6.m: Sūta said: / Kaśyapa had another ascetic wife named Danu; / tormented by grief for her sons, she came to Diti's residence.
Weeping, she bowed down to the pair of lotus feet; / when she arrived in great distress, Diti addressed her:
Diti said: / "O blessed lady, what is this cause of your weeping? / In the world, noble women are considered mothers with even a single son,
whereas you, fair lady, are the mother of a hundred virtuous sons! / You are the mother, auspicious one, of great souls like Śumbha.
Why have you incurred sorrow? Tell me the reason for this. / King Hiraṇyakaśipu and the immensely powerful Hiraṇyākṣa—
you whose two sons are great souls of immense strength and prowess, / why has great sorrow arisen? Therefore, friend, speak!
Relate the whole cause for which you weep now." / Having addressed that goddess thus, the wise lady paused.
Danu said: / "Look, look, blessed lady, at the wish of our co-wife! / It has been fulfilled by that wielder of the discus, the god of gods.
Just as a boon was previously granted to Aditi by Viṣṇu, O goddess, / even so a great boon has now been granted for her son.
A famous son was born from Kaśyapa, the protector of the three worlds; / the rank of Indra was given to him, having wrested it away from your son.
Her desires fulfilled, Aditi has her joy increased; / and now her younger son, Vasudatta,

enjoys the position of Indra, which is exceedingly hard to attain, together with the gods."
Diti said: / "Why has my wise son fallen from his position?
And how have the other dānavas and daityas been stripped of their glory, O friend? / Tell me the reason for that at length, glorious lady!"
Having addressed those words to her, Diti fell silent, deeply distressed. / Danu said: / "All the gods and dānavas, filled with wrath, entered into battle.
There a great battle took place, causing the destruction of the Daityas. / And by the gods and by Viṣṇu in battle my sons were struck down.
Likewise your sons were [struck down] by the discus-wielding God of gods, / just as a lion would put to flight those in the forest by its own splendor.
So were those sons of mine slain by the conch-handed one. / The army led by Kālanemi, invincible to gods and asuras,
was entirely destroyed, crushed, routed, and broken, / just as fire with its own flames burns the grass in a forest.
Even so Keśava burns all the hosts of Daityas. / O goddess, my sons have died, as have your many sons.
Just as all moths perish upon reaching fire, / even so all those Dānavas perished upon reaching Hari.
Thus indeed Diti heard this dreadful narrative. / Diti said: 'O auspicious one, why do you speak to me in this way like the falling of a thunderbolt?'
Addressing her thus, that goddess fell down unconscious: / 'Alas, alas! This misery has arisen, causing great sorrow and torment!'
Then, sorely afflicted with grief for her sons, she wept piteously. / Seeing her, that best of sages spoke auspicious words:
'Do not weep; may it be well with you! Those like you do not mourn thus, / [for they are] endowed with sattva, O fortunate one, and free from greed and delusion.
Whose sons, indeed, are in this worldly existence, O goddess? Whose are good kinsmen? / No one belongs to anyone; hear all about that, my dear.
You are also Dakṣa's daughters, beautiful, and thus mine. / I am your husband, the fulfiller of desires, O auspicious one,
the uniter, the cherisher, and the protector, O fair-faced woman. / Why was enmity made by the cruel asuras whose minds were uncontrolled?
Your sons, O fortunate one, were devoid of truth and righteousness. / By that fault, and indeed by your fault, O auspicious one,
they were slain by Vāsudeva and struck down by the deities. / Therefore, grief should not be indulged in, which destroys truth and liberation.
For grief destroys merit, and from the depletion of merit one perishes. / Therefore abandon grief, which is the nature of an obstacle, O fair-faced one.
By the power of their own fault the Dānavas met with death; / the gods were merely the instrumental cause, and they were destroyed by their own karma.
Knowing this, O fortunate one, attain happiness.' / Having spoken thus to that beloved woman afflicted with sorrow,
that great-minded one ceased from his despondency and fell silent.

2.7.m: Diti said: 'All that you have spoken is true, my lord, there is no doubt. / Abandoning affection for my husband, I have arrived at the state born of co-wives, O twice-born one.
Through arrogance, sorrow, and humiliation, O best of beings, / burning with great sorrow, I shall release my life-breaths.'
Kaśyapa said: 'Listen, I shall declare how peace will come to be. / No one is anyone’s son, nor mother, nor father, O auspicious one;
no one is anyone’s brother or relative, nor kinfolk and kinsmen. / Such is the bond of saṃsāra, conjoined with delusion and illusion.
One is one's own father, O goddess, one's own mother and relatives; / one is one's own company of kinfolk, and one is oneself the eternal dharma.
Through righteous conduct a person attains happiness, O goddess; / through unrighteous conduct and sin one surely meets destruction.
A person enters a cruel womb in this way, O goddess, without doubt, / by actions devoid of truth, by great sin, and through delusion.
When a mortal constantly acts in enmity toward living beings, / enemies await him wherever he may be, without doubt.
When a mortal acts with friendliness in the world, O dear and auspicious one, / then friends indeed appear for him everywhere, O passionate lady.
When a farmer, O goddess, properly plants hidden seed, / just whatever kind it is, such is the fruit he enjoys.
So too rivalry was made by your sons with virtuous beings. / The fruit of that action has been obtained; experience it firmly.
Your sons, O fortunate one, were devoid of austerity and peace. / Through that sin they have all fallen from their exalted state.
Knowing this, attain tranquility; cast off sorrow and also joy. / Whose are sons and friends? Whose are kinfolk and relatives?
Living beings live happily in accordance with their own actions. / Worrying about another's sake, O goddess, wise men possessing knowledge of reality
do not do, O noble-minded one; it is entirely useless, without doubt. / The body consists of the five elements, merely worn out at the joints.
By him all was made into a friend of the Self, O goddess, with the hope of happiness. / That which is called the Self is highly sacred, omnipresent, and all-seeing,
possessing all perfections, the Self of all, sattvic, the bestower of all accomplishments. / Thus he, consisting of everything, wanders alone, untainted, O goddess.
As he wandered alone, O best of twice-borns, / four sacred embodied beings possessing great energy were shown [to him].
And the fifth was breath, the friend of the earlier ones. / Then the Self approached, or rather the aid of knowledge.
Seeing them, that great-souled Self indeed said to knowledge: / 'O knowledge, behold these five deliberating with one another.
Having gone to them, do you speak and ask, "Who are you?"' / Hearing the supreme and meaningful words of that great-souled one,
then [knowledge] said to the adorable Self: 'What is your purpose with them? / Tell me in truth, O god; you are always and forever pure.'
The Self said: 'These five are fortunate, possessing form and intelligent. / Having gone, I shall show myself to them; listen, O knowledge, as I address [them].
I shall speak to these noble ones who have reached the fifth state. / Go as a messenger, O knowledge, skilled in the duty of an envoy.'
Knowledge said: 'O Self, listen to my words; I speak truth, absolute truth. / An association with these must never be formed by you, dear one.
Even with these five, it should not be formed by the pure-souled one desiring auspiciousness. / Through delusion one desires association with them, O great-minded one.'
The Self said: 'O knowledge, why do you prevent association with them? / Tell me that reason truly, O learned one.'
Knowledge said: 'Merely from contact with them, great sorrow will arise. / For the five are indeed the root of sorrow, the causes of grief and anguish.'
'So be it, O very wise one, I shall do your bidding.' / Having thus spoken to knowledge, that Self united with meditation.
Kaśyapa said: 'Then those very five saw that Self there. / Calling Intellect, they said: "Do you indeed approach the Self.
Act as an envoy, O auspicious lady, for us with the Self. / The five great-souled principles, auspicious upholders of the universe,
desire your friendship." Thus addressing that high-minded one, / [they said:] "Having gone, O Intellect, your duty is to be performed; go forth from here."'
'So be it, O fortunate ones, I shall perform the excellent duty.' / Having spoken thus to them, she went and said to that Self:
'I am Intellect, O fortunate one, having approached you / on an embassy from the presence of the great ones; hear their message.
The five beings desire imperishable friendship with you. / Make friends, O very wise one, and abandon meditation far away.'
Meditation said: / You must not form an association with these, O Self! / Merely by contact with them, great suffering will arise.
Deprived of me, Knowledge, how will you perform action? / Therefore, you must never form an association with them.
They will lead you into dwelling in a womb; it cannot be otherwise, O lord. / Deprived of me, Knowledge, you will surely lapse into ignorance.
Having thus spoken to that self of great intellect, [Meditation] fell silent. / Then the Self, having resolved, spoke to that Intellect who had arrived:
"Knowledge and Meditation are my two noble, excellent ministers; / it is not fitting for me to go there. What, then, shall I do, O Intellect?"
Having heard this, the renowned Intellect / reported in full to them that discourse of Knowledge and Meditation.
Then all those five [elements] approached the Self: / "We surely desire friendship with you forever.
Because you are pure, O lord of the world, therefore we have approached you. / Deliberating for yourself, let an answer be given to us."
The Self said: / "You five have arrived and desire friendship with me; / state your qualities and power before me."
Earth said: / "I am the foundation of all activity, endowed with skin and flesh; / mine is the firmness of the base of bones, endowed with nails and hair.
My power indeed, O greatly wise one, lies within the body. / Scent, moving through the nostrils, is my high-minded servant."
Ether said: / "I, Ether, have arrived. Hear my power within the body, / which has the nature of the supreme Brahman, as I declare it.
I am the external and internal space, and I dwell in empty regions. / There, my two ears are established as ministers for the purpose of hearing."
Wind said: / "I abide in fivefold form and bring about good and evil in this way. / The skin, established in the body as my minister, resorts to the quality of touch."
Fire said: / "Always established in the body, I perpetually carry out digestion. / I reveal all things, both external and internal, substance and non-substance.
Semen, marrow, and likewise saliva, as well as blood situated in the joints of the skin— / residing within the body, I dispatch them all.
There, the two eyes are my ministers who accomplish the apprehension of objects. / Thus has my supreme activity been related before you."
Water said: / "I constantly satisfy the body with nectar. / Such is my activity there, O dear one, in the city of the body.
Know the tongue to be my minister, bringing the supreme savoring of tastes." / The Nose said: / "Through pleasant fragrance, I also provide supreme nourishment to the body.
Rejecting bad odor, I display fragrance in the body. / Joined with intellect, O fortunate one, and animated by its disposition,
I remain steady in this body for the work of my master. / Know fragrance, which proceeds in two ways, to be my quality."
The two ears said: / "Dwelling in our own body, we hear sound, proper and improper action, / the good and evil spoken by people, the true and false, the pleasant and unpleasant.
Sound is declared to be our quality, and indeed our function. / Without doubt, I employ it whenever Intellect supplies it."
The Skin said: / "Wind consisting of a fivefold nature is arranged in this body.
I know in truth their activity, both external and internal: / cold and heat, sunshine, rain, and the vibration of the wind.
I know every contact—embrace, clinging, and so forth—among men. / Touch alone is my quality; I state this as truth.
Thus indeed has my function been recounted to you." / The two eyes said: / "Whatever forms there are in the world, beautiful and unbeautiful, O best of beings,
we see them only when Intellect impels us, not otherwise. / We dwell within the body; form is our quality here.
Such is the connection of our activity within the body, O intelligent one." / The Tongue said: / "Joined with intellect, O dear one, I discern the distinctions of tastes:
saline, sour, and so forth; I contemplate all that is flavorless and savory. / Constantly engaged through this activity, I dwell here.
For Intellect is the leader of all sense faculties. / Thus the five sense faculties arrived, O dear one, hear!
They declared their own respective tasks again and again. / Then Intellect arrived and said to that intelligent one:
"When the body is deprived of me, it perishes; not otherwise. / Therefore, relying upon me, conduct yourself, O intelligent one!"
Then Action arrived and said this to the Self: / "I am Action, O greatly wise one, who have come to your side.
I dispatch you along that path by which you go in this world." / Having heard all that, the Self spoke to them:
"You are joined with the fivefold elements, common indeed to all. / Why do you desire friendship in that fivefold assembly?
Let all of you tell all the reason before me!" / The fivefold elements said: / "From association with us, the physical body is born.
In that body, O one of great intellect and good vows, you dwell. / And by your grace we all abide there.
For this reason we constantly desire friendship with you." / The Self said: / "So be it, O fortunate ones! That which is dear to you
I will do, without a doubt; friendship arises for the sake of affection." / Though restrained by the great-souled Knowledge
and by Meditation, that great self entered into their company. / Deluded there by them through attachment, aversion, and the rest,
the lord, joined with the five elements, attained the state of being embodied. / When he entered the womb, filled with feces and urine,
foul-smelling, a whirlpool of slime, he fell, united with them. / Agitated in his body, he spoke to the fivefold elements:
"O all you fivefold elements, listen to my words! / Through association with you, I am confounded by great suffering.
Indeed, I have fallen into this slimy, terrible, great terror!" / The fivefold elements said: / "O king, remain as long as the womb fills out.
Afterward, your exit will surely occur, without a doubt. / For you are our master, established in the realm of the body.
Sovereignty must be exercised in this way; you will become the enjoyer of pleasures." / Hearing their words, the Self, tormented with sorrow,
wishing to go, became intent on fleeing from that place.

2.8.m: Kaśyapa said: / Agitated in the womb, grieving day by day, / overcome with sorrow, the righteous self was tormented by every affliction.
Hanging head downwards in the womb, bound by the snare of delusion, / overwhelmed by mental and physical illnesses, he wailed in distress, insensate.
Pervaded by great grief, afflicted, he spoke to Knowledge: / The Self said: / "I did not heed your word then, O greatly wise one!
Though held back by Meditation, I fell into the crisis of delusion. / Therefore save me, O greatly wise one, from this dreadful dwelling in a womb!"
Knowledge said: / "You were restrained by me, O Self, yet you did not heed my word. / By the very cruel fivefold elements, you were cast into the crisis of the womb.
"Go now to meditation; from it you will obtain happiness. / There is no doubt: you will indeed attain liberation from dwelling in the womb."
Having heard those words of his, and understanding the true nature of knowledge, / he called upon meditation and said: "Listen to my words:
I have come to you for refuge, O meditation! Protect me constantly!" / "So be it, O very wise one!" meditation said to the great-minded one.
Having heard these words, the self indeed attained meditation; / accompanied by meditation in the womb, he remained free of delusion.
When the self attained meditation, the fear born of the womb was forgotten; / joined with the two good [companions, knowledge and meditation], the self there was separated from delusion.
Constantly contemplating the innate bliss of the self: / "As soon as I have exited from here, I will cast off this body made of the five elements."
The master, while dwelling in the womb, constantly reflected thus. / But when the time of delivery arrived, O fair-faced woman, through the wind of Prajāpati,
the embryo was moved by the wind, and by the exceedingly powerful prāṇa. / The birth-canal then undergoes an expansion of twenty-four finger-breadths,
while the embryo is twenty-five finger-breadths; therefore, intense pain is produced. / Thus being severely squeezed, he swooned in a faint, O beloved.
Endowed with knowledge and meditation, he fell upon the surface of the earth, / separated [from them] by the divine wind of Prajāpati.
At the mere touch of the earth, both knowledge and meditation were forgotten. / Bewildered by the bondage of saṃsāra, the self remained steeped in attachments.
Overpowered by virtues and faults, filled with great delusion, / day by day he desires only food, drink, and the like.
Thus being nourished together with the five elements, / the self was pervaded by all the senses and by sin-producing sense objects.
Through delusion regarding kin, and likewise regarding wife and others, / he becomes, O goddess, perturbed and distracted day by day.
Perplexed by great delusion, the master was caught in the net of delusion, / just as a fish is bound by a fisherman with the bindings of a net.
He was not able to move at all; thus was the self bound fast, / bound by all those nets of delusion, with tight bonds.
He was pervaded by this unfolding phenomenal world, though [himself] the all-pervader; / fallen from knowledge and discernment, smitten by passion, hatred, and the like.
Tormented by desire, and likewise indeed by anger, / bound by material nature and by karma, he became utterly deluded.
Sūta said: / When the self, having thus become foolish, fell under the sway of desire and anger, / he was occupied by all those wicked [states], greed, passion, and the like:
"This is my wife; this is my son; this is my friend; this is my house"— / in this way, he was bound by the net of saṃsāra, by great delusion.
Distressed then by various sufferings, such as sorrow over a son, / and seized by old age, by diseases, and likewise by mental agonies,
the self was thus deeply tormented by terrible sorrows and delusions, / shattered by pride, by humiliations, and by various griefs.
Afflicted by old age, O goddess, and likewise by infirmity, / he continually broods over sorrow, crying "Alas! Alas!", bereft of consciousness.
At night he would see dreams; by day he was devoid of awareness, / overwhelmed day by day, O goddess, by the debility of his limbs.
As he wandered in saṃsāra, dispassion was revealed to him there: / fearless, free of kin, tranquil, and contented.
Then the self said to him who was free from desire and anger: / "Who are you in naked form? Why are you not ashamed before friends,
where there are people—old women, young maidens, and mothers? / Having gone into their midst, are you not afraid uncovered?"
The dispassionate one said: / "Who is seen here as naked? I am never naked! / You yourself are well bound, though provided with clothing.
I am never naked, O divine one; you appear naked, / acting under the sway of sense objects, devoid of propriety!"
The self said: / "What indeed is propriety for a man? Declare that, O one of good vows, / in detail, O very wise one, if you know it for certain."
The dispassionate one, very wise and great-minded, said to him: / "The mind constantly maintains firm steadfastness in pleasures and pains,
and whatever has been tormented by all conditions, one should abandon in each of them. / Now I shall explain shame, which enters fully into the mind:
'This must not be done by me today.' Being naked, deprived of his station, / deeply absorbed in repentance—that is called shame.
Before whom should shame be felt? There is never a second [being]. / And there is only one divine person; what would he destroy of anyone?
Now I shall speak of the people who have been mentioned by you: / Just as a potter places a lump of clay upon the wheel,
and having turned it, by means of a cord, reveals various distinct forms / of thousands of vessels according to his will, his mind firmly focused,
even so does this Creator fashion diverse forms, not otherwise; / afterwards, they meet with destruction for some reason or other.
Those which are always abiding, and which are eternal worlds— / shame should be felt before them; indeed, they do not return to earth.
Space, wind, fire, earth, and water as the fifth— / these are the worlds that shine forth, which are situated everywhere.
These five are well situated in the limbs of living beings; / they exist everywhere. Before whom is shame prescribed?
I shall explain the nature of women; listen now, my dear friend. / Just as in thousands of jars filled with water,
the one moon shines everywhere, even so do you shine, / entering thousands of living beings in the wheel of delusion, O great-souled one!
And you reside in all stationary and moving beings alike, / through the sinful gateway of the womb, full of māyā and delusion.
Through two breasts and two hips, and through youth she shines forth; / and here an excess growth of chest-flesh is seen, no doubt.
A form of delusion has been displayed for the downfall of living beings. / She who has been spoken of by you is not truly a woman at all.
The Creator makes [her] in play, always for his own amusement. / Just as in a woman, so in a man the living soul resides everywhere.
Those who are devoid of breasts and womb are always the living-liberated. / Man is declared to be the spirit (puruṣa); woman is called material nature (prakṛti).
He indeed sports with her; she is never liberated. / Joined with material nature, you are seen among men.
Who feels shame before whom? Knowing this, walk in happiness! / I shall explain the old woman, the eternally old one, O fair-faced lady:
whose skin on her limbs has become withered, O fair-faced lady, / and who is covered with white and grey hair,
destitute of strength, wretched, and covered with wrinkles then— / this is not the old woman; another is called old.
The characteristic of that one has been described; I now speak of the young woman. / Constantly growing through knowledge, taking refuge at the side of the individual soul,
she is named 'good discernment' (sumati); she is both the old woman and the young woman, / established always among men and women in the worlds.
Shame should be felt before her; and I shall declare another thing. / I shall indeed explain the mother who was mentioned by you:
Consciousness resides constantly in the bodies of living beings, / and that which bestows supreme knowledge is called wisdom (prajñā).
Discernment is proclaimed as the mother; she is established / for the protection of living beings in all the worlds, for their nourishment and welfare.
The one called right-mindedness is proclaimed as the mother; / all the forms that constantly lead along the path to the gates of saṃsāra,
these indeed become mothers who reveal manifold sorrow. / Thus the form of the mother has been explained. What else shall I tell you?
The Self said: / Who are you that have arrived, destroyer of my anguish? / Explain to me in detail your own essential nature.
Freedom-from-Attachment said: / [I am he] from whom desires turn away, all of them becoming hopeless, / whom people, out of malice, do not see—these actions are not otherwise;
near whom longing never approaches at all, / and through fear of whom anger, greed, and delusion have perished.
I am Freedom-from-Attachment, may you be blessed; Discernment is my kinsman. / The Self said: What is he like, this brother of yours named Discernment?
Describe to me the characteristics of that brother and of yourself. / Freedom-from-Attachment said: I will not merely describe his characteristics and form before you;
O fortunate one, I will call that brother myself. / O Discernment, my brother, listen to our words!
Come, come, O most fortunate one, out of love for me, O highly intelligent one! / Kaśyapa said: Accompanied by his two wives, Tranquility and Forbearance, he arrived—
all-seeing, all-pervading, omnipresent, devoted to all truths, / the enemy of all doubts, affectionate toward knowledge.
Retention and Intellect were the two daughters of that great soul, / and Yoga was his eldest son, whose supreme master is liberation.
Stainless, free from ego, free from desire, devoid of possessions, / serene in mind at all times, beyond the pairs of opposites, of great intellect,
that Discernment arrived, adorned with the jewels of virtues, / whose two noble and wise ministers were Dharma and Truth.
Accompanied by Forbearance and Tranquility, that Discernment arrived / and spoke thus to Freedom-from-Attachment: 'Summoned by you, I have come;
therefore, brother, let the whole reason be told to me, / relying upon which you have just now summoned me.'
Freedom-from-Attachment said: / This person standing before us is bound fast by great snares, / bewildered by the arrows of delusion and by the fetters of saṃsāra.
He is the all-pervading master, this Self of mine, / pervaded by the five elements, destitute of knowledge and meditation.
Question this Self, since you are learned in the true principles. / Hearing the words of Freedom-from-Attachment, Discernment spoke:
Discernment said: / Do you abide in happiness, O Lord, ruler of the universe? / Having arrived in saṃsāra, what happiness have you yourself enjoyed?
The Self said: / Dwelling in the womb was a great, unbearable, terrible suffering / that I have experienced, O exceedingly wise one, being ever devoid of knowledge.
In the body too, fallen from knowledge, I became many things; / then, having reached the state of childhood, I committed what should and should not be done.
In youth, play was indulged in, and a wife was enjoyed many times; / reaching old age, I was tormented by grief for sons and the like.
By separations from wife and kin I am scorched day and night; / by sorrows of manifold kinds I am tormented day after day.
Day and night, O wise one, I find no happiness anywhere; / thus exceedingly tormented by sorrows, what shall I do, O high-minded one?
Tell me that expedient by which I may indeed find happiness; / free me today from this flood of worldly traps, from this strong bondage.
Discernment said: / You are pure, beyond dualities, and sinless, O lord of the world; / go to this great soul, Freedom-from-Attachment, who gives happiness.
Undoubtedly you have seen him—naked, devoid of outward ritual; / for he reveals happiness and destroys all anguish.
Hearing this, the pure Self went back to Freedom-from-Attachment; / sighing and miserable, he said to him: 'Listen to my words:
show me that path by which I may find happiness.' / [Freedom-from-Attachment said:] 'So be it, O very wise one, I shall do as you say;
go again to Discernment, for you had conversation about happiness with him; / he will indeed be the teacher of the path of happiness for you.'
Sent by meritorious Freedom-from-Attachment, the Lord went, / and spoke to that great-souled Discernment, the best of the pure:
'Show me happiness; indeed, I was sent by Freedom-from-Attachment; / having taken refuge in you, save me from terrible saṃsāra.'
Discernment said: / 'Go to Knowledge, O very wise one; he will tell you everything.' / Thus addressed, the Self reached the place where Knowledge was established.
[The Self said:] / 'O Knowledge of great splendor, revealer of all truths, / I have taken refuge in you; reveal to me the path of happiness.'
Knowledge said: / 'I am your servant, O Lord of the world; do you not recognize me, O keeper of noble vows? / Previously, by means of meditation, you were restrained by me again and again.
Through association with the five elements you have fallen into calamity; / go to Meditation, O wise one, and he will grant you happiness.'
Sent by Knowledge, the Self stood taking refuge in Meditation: / 'Meditation, show me that happiness which is absolute and perfected;
protect me, who have thus come to your refuge!' / Hearing those words spoken by him,
Meditation, highly gladdened, spoke in turn to that Self: / 'I am not to be abandoned, my dear, firmly resolved in all actions;
accompanied by Freedom-from-Attachment and Discernment, always / become endowed with meditation and behold your Self!
Possessed of the Self, becoming steady, free from distress, beyond conceptualization, / just as a lamp set in a windless place burns steadily without flickering,
so having burned away faults, one indeed attains nirvana. / Remaining in solitude, abstaining from food, or eating moderately at all times,
free from dualities, devoid of sounds, seated motionless on your seat, / meditating on the Self by means of the Self, with intellect fixed on me alone,
you shall attain the supreme abode, that highest place of Viṣṇu.'

2.9.m: Kaśyapa said: / Thus instructed there by Meditation and the others at that time, / that wise Self, desiring to abandon that fivefold body-effect,
seeing only the instrumental causes, having attained them, departs; / having cast aside the body as unworthy of regard, when it has fallen, he does not look back at it.
There is no lasting connection between the vital breath and the body, though nurtured together; / by what cause then could there be any connection with wealth, sons, and wives?
Knowing this, attain tranquility; do not give in to weakness, O beloved! / He alone is the Supreme Brahman; he alone is the eternal one;
he resides within the demons and the gods in the form of the Self; / he is Brahmā, he is Rudra, and he is eternal Viṣṇu;
he creates the universes, he protects the creatures, / and he destroys them—this righteous one, Janārdana whose form is dharma.
By him the gods were produced, and the demons as well, O beloved; / the gods are freed by dharma, while your sons are devoid of dharma.
This dharma is a limb of Mādhava, protected by all the gods; / therefore, O goddess, one should contemplate dharma and truly uphold dharma.
To him Viṣṇu, the righteous soul, is always gracious. / Indeed, the gods conduct themselves in dharma, in truth, and in asceticism.
With those with whom Viṣṇu is pleased, dharma is protected by them here in this world. / This dharma is the body of Viṣṇu, and truth is his very heart.
Viṣṇu is pleased with him who constantly maintains those two. / He who corrupts truth and dharma fosters only sin.
Viṣṇu becomes enraged with him; exceedingly powerful, he destroys him. / Dharma is protected by the Vaiṣṇavas who abide in asceticism and truth.
The righteous soul is pleased with them, and thus grants protection. / Your sons, the sons of Danu, and likewise the Saiṃhikeyas,
behaving with unrighteousness and sin, their minds evil, / were slain in battle by Vāsudeva holding the discus in hand.
That self which was spoken of by me earlier in your presence, / that is this Viṣṇu, without doubt, the righteous soul, protector of all.
Dwelling within the bodies of the Daityas, established in sin itself, / he, very wise, became enraged, O queen, and struck down the Dānavas.
Becoming both external and internal, your sons were struck down. / And by whom they were generated, O queen, by him indeed they were cast down.
No delusion should be entertained regarding them by you; listen to my word: / whoever behaves with sin, that very one goes to destruction.
Therefore, abandoning delusion, always resort to dharma.' / Diti said: 'Let it be so, highly fortunate one; I shall do your bidding.'
Having thus addressed Kaśyapa, best of sages, the sorrowful woman, / enlightened by the sage, abandoned her sorrow and remained [calm].

2.10.m: The sages said: / 'Then what course of action did all those Dānavas, led by Hiraṇyakaśipu, / broken in battle, undertake, O highly wise one?
Tell us at length of their supreme conduct; / we all wish to hear it now from you, O twice-born one.'
Sūta said: / 'Broken from the battle, all of them devoid of strength at that time, / their pride gone, deeply afflicted with sorrow, those Daityas went to their father.
Bowing down with devotion, all of them then said to Kaśyapa: / The Dānavas said: 'From your semen is our origin, O best of the twice-born,
and of the deities as well, O highly fortunate one, and of the Dānavas. / And we Dānavas are all endowed with strength, vigour, and valour,
knowing means, very steadfast, and endowed with effort. / But we are many, father, while the gods are few.
How is it that they all conquer and we are broken from the great battle? / What indeed is the cause of that, father, [when we are] endowed with strength and brilliance?
Each single Daitya, O highly wise one, possesses the strength / of thousands of elephants in rut; there is no such [strength] among the gods.
Yet victory is seen only among the gods in the great battle, father. / Tell us all that; you should dispel our doubt.'
Kaśyapa said: / 'Listen, all my sons, to the cause of victory, / on account of which all the deities became victorious in battle.
The father is the caster of the seed, while the mother is ever this field; / so it is indeed in holding, in protecting, and in nourishing.
What could a father do in a diverse matter, even regarding a son? / Here action alone is primary; thus has my intellect concluded.
The connection of action is twofold, arising from sin and merit. / Relying on truth alone, supreme dharma is performed.
Combined with asceticism and meditation, it is conducive to deliverance, O sons; / sin is declared to cause downfall always, there is no doubt.
By strength, by retinue, and by noble birth, O sons, / for a man devoid of merit, that strength becomes impaired.
There are tall trees in mountain fortresses, O good sons; / they fall down with roots together by the force of the wind, dense as they are.
Those devoid of truth and dharma go likewise to Yama's abode. / And this dharma is common to all living beings, O good sons,
by which a creature crosses over both here and in the hereafter. / That truth endowed with dharma was abandoned by you.
Unrighteousness was resorted to, O sons, by you who are devoid of truth. / Fallen from truth, dharma, and asceticism, you have fallen into an ocean of sorrow.
And the gods are endowed with truth and endowed with welfare, / possessed of asceticism, tranquility, and self-restraint, exceedingly virtuous, and free from sin.
Where there is truth and dharma, and likewise asceticism and merit, / and where Viṣṇu Hṛṣīkeśa is, there victory is seen.
Eternal Vāsudeva has become their ally; / therefore those gods, endowed with truth and dharma, conquer.
With an ally, with strength, and likewise with human effort— / indeed, O sons, you are devoid of asceticism and truth.
He who has Viṣṇu as ally, and likewise asceticism and strength, / his victory alone is seen; thus know the knowers of dharma.
You, however, are devoid of dharma and devoid of asceticism and truth; / previously you attained Indra's station by force alone.
Without asceticism, O very wise ones, without dharma, without fame, / Indra's station is not to be attained by the qualities of strength and pride, O sons.
Even having attained Indra's station, O sons, they fall from it indeed. / Therefore, perform asceticism, O sons, united together,
endowed with freedom from hostility, endowed with knowledge and meditation; / and enmity should never be made with Keśava.
When, O sons, you become blessed like this, / then you all will attain supreme perfection; there is no doubt.'
Thus addressed by the great-souled Kaśyapa, / those Dānavas of great majesty, hearing their father's speech,
bowed down to Kaśyapa with devotion, stood up, and filled with haste, / those Daityas held good counsel, assembled among themselves.
King Hiraṇyakaśipu then spoke to those Dānavas: / 'We shall perform severe asceticism that grants all things.'
Hiraṇyākṣa then said: 'I shall perform fierce asceticism; / then by force I shall seize the three worlds, there is no doubt here.
Having conquered Govinda in battle, that evil-minded one, / and having destroyed all the deities, I shall attain Indra's station.'
Bali said: 'It is not fitting for you to act thus, O lords of the sons of Diti; / that enmity which is with Viṣṇu, that enmity is the cause of destruction.
By acts of giving, dharma, merit, austerities, and the performance of sacrifices, / men go to happiness after worshipping that Hṛṣīkeśa.'
Hiraṇyakaśipu said: / 'I myself will never perform the worship of Hari. / Abandoning one's innate nature, should the service of an enemy be practiced?
The wise consider that indeed worse than death. / The service of Viṣṇu should not be done by me or by the other Dānavas.'
Bali again spoke to that great-souled grandfather: / 'Whatever has been seen in the Dharmaśāstras by sages who know the truth,
the counsel endowed with statecraft, especially concerning an enemy: / knowing oneself to be inferior, and that enemy to be strong,
one should go to his side and await the time of victory; / darkness always dwells resorting to the shadow of a lamp.'
Seeing that the oil of the lamp has reached the wick, its light departs swiftly, / and once again the great power of darkness increases.
In the same way, one should conciliate in secret, pointing out affection truly, / having formed an affectionate bond with the gods through righteous intentions, O enemies of the gods!
Indeed, such excellent counsel was formerly spoken by the sage Kaśyapa. / Self-possessed, O king of kings, accomplish your task by that counsel!"
Hearing his word, the majestic Daitya said: / "O grandson, I will not do this, causing my own dishonour!
And all the other kinsmen spoke to that scholar of conduct: / "What Bali has said is meritorious and pleases the gods;
it confers honor on Indra, but brings fear to the Dānavas. / We all shall perform supreme asceticism alone.
Having vanquished the gods by asceticism, we will seize our own realm." / Thus deliberating together, having rejected Bali at that time,
the great Asuras, harboring great enmity toward Viṣṇu in their hearts, / then all practiced asceticism in the mountain fastnesses and on the peaks.
Thus all those Dānavas, shedding desire, firmly resolved, / free from lust and anger, abstaining from food, conquered fatigue.

2.11.m: The sages said: / "You, omniscient one, have recounted the battle between the Daityas and Dānavas. / Now we wish to hear about the high-souled Suvrata.
Whose son was that wise one, and in whose lineage was he born? / What was the asceticism of that Brahmin, and how was Hari propitiated [by him]?"
Sūta said: / "Just as the narrative was heard by me of old through the power of wisdom, / even so, O Brahmins, I will declare the story of the high-souled Suvrata,
his holy, divine, and auspicious Vaiṣṇava conduct / before you all, entirely through the grace of Viṣṇu.
In a previous kalpa, O fortunate ones, in a holy land that destroys sin, / on the sacred bank of the Revā, at the sacred site named Vāmana,
a best of Brahmins named Somaśarman was born in the family of Kuśika. / But he was childless and overwhelmed by much grief.
Constantly tormented by poverty and sorrow, / he would ponder day and night the means to obtain a son and wealth.
Once, however, his beloved, a virtuous woman named Sumanā, / observed her husband dejected with his face downcast due to worry.
Seeing her beloved then, the ascetic woman said to him: / "Your mind is overwhelmed by countless nets of sorrow.
You are bewildered by delusion; cast off your worry, O highly intelligent one! / Disclose your sorrow to me; become composed and attain happiness!
There is no misery like anxiety, for it emaciates the body. / He who lives having abandoned anxiety rejoices in happiness.
Declare before me, O Brahmin, the cause of your anxiety." / Having heard the words of his beloved, Somaśarman said to his wife:
Somaśarman said: / "Worry brought on by longing, O blessed lady, is the cause of sorrow. / I will explain all that; listen and understand!
I do not know by what sin I am destitute of wealth, O virtuous one, / and likewise bereft of a son; this is the cause of my sorrow."
Sumanā said: / "Listen, I shall proclaim the destruction of all doubt, / the essential nature of instruction, the vision of all knowledge.
Greed is indeed the seed of sin, and delusion is its root; / falsehood is its trunk, and deception its widespread branches;
hypocrisy and crookedness are its leaves; it is ever in bloom with evil intellect; / unfaithfulness is its fragrance, and ignorance alone is its fruit;
fraud, heresy, hostility, envy, cruelty, and crookedness—these sinners / are birds residing in the illusory branches of the tree of delusion;
ignorance is its delicious fruit, and adharma is the sap of that fruit; / nurtured with the water of craving, disbelief is its delightful sap;
adharma is its sweet juice, which appears violently delicious. / Such are the fruits borne by the tree of greed.
The man who, resorting to its shade, is fully satisfied, / eats its well-ripened fruits day after day;
and nurtured by the juice of its fruits, by adharma, / that mortal, becoming content, proceeds toward his fall.
Therefore, setting aside worry, a man should not indulge in greed; / he should not give way to anxiety over wealth, sons, or wives.
When one who is wise walks in the path of fools, O beloved, / like a fool he constantly worries: 'How can wealth become mine?
How can I obtain a good wife, and how can I gain sons?' / Thus, being bewildered, he worries continually day and night.

For a moment in the midst of worry he may perceive great happiness, / but then returning to consciousness, he is tormented by great sorrow.

Abandoning anxiety and delusion, conduct yourself rightly, O Brahmin! / In saṃsāra there is no lasting relation with anyone, O wise one!
Friends, kinsmen, sons, fathers, mothers, servants, / and wives alike are merely transient relations.
Somaśarman said: / "What kind of relation is it, O blessed one? Tell me in detail, / by which all—wealth, sons, and kinsmen—become connected to us."
Sumanā said: / "Some are related through debt; some are stealers of deposits; / some bestow profits, while others are neutral.
In these four divisions are sons, friends, women, / wives, fathers, mothers, servants, relatives, and kinsfolk born.
They are born upon the earth according to their respective connections. / When one has misappropriated a deposit belonging to another in this world,
the owner of that deposit becomes a virtuous and handsome son on earth, / born without doubt in the house of the very one who stole the deposit.
The owner of the deposit, having departed after suffering terrible grief from the theft of his deposit, / became a good son to the embezzler of the deposit.
Virtuous, handsome, and endowed with all auspicious marks, / showing devotion to him, he lives as his son day after day,
speaking pleasant words, gentle, sickly, showing immense affection, / seizing his own wealth [by expenses] and generating excellent affection [in his father].
Just as intense, life-destroying sorrow was formerly caused / by the embezzler through the theft of the deposit, O fortunate one,
even so, having become a son possessing great virtues through that friendship, / he becomes short-lived and goes to his death.
Having inflicted grief, he departs thus, being born again and again. / When that [father] wails, 'Alas, my son! My son!',
[the departed spirit] laughs, thinking: 'Whose son is anyone, and who is the father? / The deposit that was mine, a means of sustenance, was stolen by this man.
Through the misappropriation of my wealth, did not my life depart formerly / in great and truly unbearable grief?
In that same way, having inflicted grief and reclaimed my excellent wealth, / I shall depart swiftly today. Whose son am I in such a manner?
He is not my father, nor was anyone ever anyone's son before. / The state of a ghost has been inflicted by me upon this wicked-souled man.'
Having spoken thus, mocking him repeatedly, he departs. / By this path he departs, having inflicted the most terrible grief.
Such sons indeed belong to one who embezzles a deposit, beloved; / in this worldly existence, they are seen here and there to be full of misery.
I shall explain to you the sons bound by debt.

2.12.m: Sumanā said: / I shall describe before you a son connected through debt; / having taken whose debt one indeed meets death,
that creditor is born as a son, a brother, a father, or a beloved wife, / or behaves under the guise of a friend, but is ever exceedingly wicked.
Cruel, of harsh appearance, he would never see any virtue; / he always speaks harsh words among his own relatives.
He eats only the sweetest foods and constantly enjoys pleasures; / always devoted to gambling, he has a craving for theft.
he consumes the property of the household by force; when restrained, he becomes angry; / and he reviles his father and mother day by day.
He is a driver-away, a terrifier, one who utters much harsh speech. / Having consumed that wealth in this way, he lives in comfort.
From childhood, through birth rites and the like, the cruel one seizes wealth, / and again through marriage alliances in various ways and repeatedly.
Thus wealth is acquired; indeed, [the parent] gives it to him thus: / 'House, fields, and everything are his alone, no doubt.'
Day after day he injures his father and mother / with sharp pieces [of wood], with pestles, and with all manner of exceedingly severe blows.
When that father dies, he is extremely harsh to the mother; / he becomes devoid of affection and cruel, without any doubt.
He never performs ancestral rites or gives gifts. / Such sons indeed arise on the face of the earth.
I shall describe to you the enemy-son, O best of the twice-born. / When he reaches childhood, he always acts with enmity.
Even while playing, he strikes his father and mother; / having struck them, he runs off, laughing again and again.
Frightened, he comes back to his father and mother; / he is constantly angry and reproaches them again and again.
Thus he constantly engages in acts of hostility at all times. / Having caused the death of his father and then of his mother,
the wicked-minded one departs, by the power of former enmity. / Now I shall explain the one from whom love is received.
As soon as he is born, he brings joy; in childhood, by fondling and games; / having grown older, he then brings joy to his mother and father.
He constantly satisfies them with devotion; he gladdens them both / with affection, with words, and with affectionate conversation.
Knowing his elder has died, he weeps again out of affection. / All the ancestral rites, the offering of rice-balls, and the rituals,
Afflicted with immense grief, he indeed performs [the duties] and provides sustenance for them; / bound by the three debts, out of affection he feeds [them] constantly.
From whom a reward is due, O dear one, he gives it, without doubt, / having become a son in this manner, O very wise one.
I will now speak before you of an indifferent one, O dear one: / he always behaves with a disposition of indifference.
He does not give, nor does he take; he neither gets angry nor is pleased; / nor does he give up anything and depart, being neutral, O best of the twice-born.
All this has been told to you: such is the nature of sons. / As is a son, so is a wife, a father, a mother, and relatives;
servants and others are also described thus, as well as cattle, horses, / elephants, female buffaloes, and slaves: these are bound by debt.
No debt was taken by him, nor by the two of us from anyone; / nor was any deposit embezzled by anyone in a previous life.
Listen, beloved, we owe a debt to no one; / nor was enmity made with anyone in a previous birth.
By the two of us, O chief of the twice-born, no one was abandoned, O husband. / Knowing this, attain peace; cast away useless anxiety.
Whose are sons? Whose is a dear wife? Whose are kinsmen and relatives? / Nothing was stolen from anyone, nor was anything given back by you.
How, then, did wealth come? Do not be bewildered! / Wherever wealth is destined to be attained, O best of the twice-born,
it comes into his very hand without effort. / And a man guards his wealth with great effort;
when he departs, he departs alone, and the wealth remains right there. / Knowing this, attain peace; cast away useless anxiety.
Whose are sons? Whose is a dear wife? Whose are kinsmen and relatives? / In this worldly existence, who belongs to whom, when there is no connection, O best of the twice-born?
Deluded by great ignorance, evil-minded men think: / 'This is my house, this is my son, these women are mine.'
This is seen to be false, beloved, a mere bond of worldly existence. / Instructed thus at that time by his devoted wife and lady,
he spoke again to his beloved wife, Sumanā, who spoke words of wisdom. / Somaśarman said: / You have spoken the truth, auspicious lady, destroying all doubts.
Nevertheless, virtuous and truly wise men desire a lineage. / Just as I have anxiety for a son, so I do for wealth, dear wife.
By whatever means possible, I shall produce a son. / Sumanā said: / Through a son one conquers worlds; a son saves the family;
through a good son, O fortunate one, the father, mother, and creatures [are saved]. / A single wise son is preferable; what is the use of many devoid of virtue?
One saves the lineage, while others cause torment. / I have already said that the others merely go after debts.
Through merit a son is obtained; through merit a noble family is obtained; / a good birth is obtained through merits; therefore, practice merit.
Death is certain for one who is born, and birth is certain for one who has died. / A good birth is obtained through merits, and so too a good death.
Happiness and heap of wealth, beloved, are enjoyed through meritorious deeds. / Somaśarman said: / Tell me the practice of merit, dear wife, and also about [good] births.
What is true merit like, auspicious one? Tell me the characteristic of merit. / Sumanā said: / First I shall describe merit, as merit was heard by me,
how a man or a woman should conduct themselves daily, / and how through merits one obtains fame, sons, loved ones, and wealth.
I shall explain all the characteristics of merit, beloved: / by chastity, truthfulness, observing the five great sacrifices,
by generosity, observances, forgiveness, and purity, dear one, / by non-violence, great capacity, and practice of non-stealing.
Through these ten limbs one should fully accomplish dharma. / Dharma becomes complete just as bodily nourishment is filled by morsels.
The righteous person generates dharma through threefold action. / With its heart pleased, dharma brings about merit for him.
Whatever the wise one reflects upon, that hard-to-attain thing he attains. / Somaśarman said: / What is the form of dharma, and what are its limbs, fair lady?
Tell me with affection, in private; faith has arisen in me to hear it. / Sumanā said: / In this world, by whom has the form of dharma ever been seen, O best of the twice-born?
Its path invisible, its essence truth, it has not been seen by gods or demons. / Born in the lineage of Atri, a twice-born, the son of Anasūyā—
By him, Dattātreya indeed, great Dharma was always seen. / But these two great-souled ones performed supreme asceticism,
Living in dharma, and by asceticism and strength, / They were to become superior in form to Indra, distinguished.
While they remained in the forest for ten thousand years, / Feeding on air, without food, they became fair to behold.
For ten thousand years, during so much time, mighty asceticism / Was being thoroughly accomplished by the two, and there Dharma became visible.
The five fires were mastered by the two for so long, O best of the twice-born; / It was accomplished at the three junctures of the day, and they abstained from food.
For that long they stood in the water—the ascetic Dattātreya, / And Durvāsas, best of sages, emaciated by asceticism.
Against Dharma that righteous one, the best among sages, grew angry. / When he, that best of sages, became enraged, O fortunate one, then—
Then Dharma arrived in his own form indeed at that time, / Endowed with celibacy and other virtues and with austerities, intelligent.
Truth in the form of a brāhmaṇa, and celibacy likewise; / Asceticism was the best of the twice-born, and Self-control was a wise, foremost twice-born.
Observance was of great wisdom, and Charitable Giving likewise; / In the form of agnihotrins they indeed approached the son of Atri.
Patience, Peace, Modesty, Non-violence, and Simplicity— / All these arrived in female forms, O best of the twice-born.
Intellect, Wisdom, Compassion, Faith, Retentive Memory, Hospitality, and Equanimity, / As well as the sacred five sacrifices, and the Vedas with their auxiliary limbs at that time,
Assuming each their own form, they all attained manifestation; / The holy rites beginning with the establishment of sacred fires, and the horse sacrifices and others,
Endowed with beauty and grace, adorned with all ornaments, / Wearing heavenly garlands and garments, anointed with divine fragrant perfumes,
Provided with diadems and earrings, adorned with divine ornaments, / Radiant, handsome, surrounded by flames of splendor—
Thus Dharma arrived, accompanied by his retinue, / Where Durvāsas was standing, wrathful like Death.
Dharma said: / Why has anger been aroused, O learned twice-born, you who are endowed with asceticism? / For anger destroys welfare and asceticism itself, without doubt.
It brings about universal ruin; therefore, one should abandon anger in this matter. / Be at ease, O best of the twice-born; highest is the fruit of asceticism.
Durvāsas said: / Who are you, who have arrived together with these foremost twice-born? / Seven women stand here, shapely and adorned.
Tell me this at length before me, O highly intelligent one. / Dharma said: / This one in the form of a brāhmaṇa, endowed with all splendor,
With a staff in his hand, very gracious, and carrying a water pot— / Behold, this is Celibacy who has come before you.
Look upon the other radiant one, O foremost twice-born, / Tawny and with reddish-brown eyes; this is Truth, O best of the twice-born.
Behold such a one, O virtuous one, with radiance equal to the Vaiśvadeva, / Who is the Asceticism that you practiced, supported by all the gods.
Behold him who has come to your side, O highly fortunate one, / Of gracious speech, full of radiance, devoted to compassion for all living beings.
This is Self-control, who always nourishes you; / Matted-haired, fierce, reddish-brown, extremely intense, a great lord,
A destroyer of sins, sword in hand, O best of the twice-born, / Deeply peaceful, of great merit, devoted to daily rituals—
Observance has arrived at your side, O best of the twice-born; / Unbound, intensely bright, resembling pure crystal,
With a water pot in his hand, a twice-born holding a tooth-stick; / This is Purity who has arrived here in your presence.
Most virtuous, highly fortunate, adorned with the ornament of truth, / Her limbs graceful with every decoration, this Service has arrived.
Exceedingly steadfast, serene of limb, fair-complexioned, with a smiling face, / Lotus in hand, this supporter, lotus-eyed, lotus-like—
Endowed with divine ornaments, Forbearance has arrived, O best of the twice-born; / Deeply tranquil, well-established, endowed with abundant auspiciousness,
Her beauty made of divine jewels, adorned with divine decorations, / Your Peace has arrived, O highly intelligent one, in the form of wisdom.
Engaged in benefiting others, filled with abundant truth, / Ever speaking measured words, this Simplicity has arrived before you.
Gracious, endowed with forbearance, adorned with all ornaments, / Seated on a lotus, shapely, dark-complexioned, renowned—
This Non-violence, highly fortunate, has approached you; / With limbs the color of molten gold, sporting red garments,
Very serene, of sacred counsel, who does not gaze aimlessly here and there, / Pervaded by a spirit of knowledge, with pure hands, practicing austerities,
Rich with the beauty of pearl ornaments, spotless, charmingly smiling— / Behold, behold, this Faith has arrived, O highly fortunate one!
Pervaded by great intellect, filled with profound wisdom, / Form inclined toward noble enjoyments, serene, beautifully auspicious,
Absorbed in meditation on all desires, mother of the world, renowned, / Rich with the beauty of all ornaments, with full hips and breasts,
