Fair of complexion, she has arrived adorned with garlands and garments; / This is Retentive Memory, O highly intelligent one, standing near you.
Resembling a swan and the moon, with dangling pearl necklaces, / Adorned with every ornament, very gracious, noble-minded,
Clothed in white garments, holding a lotus in her hand, / With a book in her lotus hand, ever radiant—
This is Wisdom, O highly fortunate one, who has approached you, the blessed one; / Bearing the color of lac-dye, ever very serene,
Wearing a garland of yellow flowers, adorned with necklaces and armlets, / Provided with finger-rings and bracelets, decorated with ear-pendants,
The goddess ever shines forth in yellow garments, / Unrivaled for the benefit and nourishment of the three worlds;
Whose virtuous character, O best of the twice-born, is ever celebrated— / That very Compassion has arrived safely at your side, O best of the twice-born.
This elderly woman, O highly intelligent one, is the ascetic wife of Bhāva; / She is my mother, O best of the twice-born, and I am Dharma, O you of noble vows.
"Knowing this, attain tranquility; protect me in this way." / Durvāsas said: "If Dharma has now approached near me,"
Tell me the reason for this: what shall I do for you, O Dharma? / Dharma said: / Why are you angry, O chief of twice-born? What unpleasant thing have they done?
Tell me the reason for that, O Durvāsas, if you deem fit. / Durvāsas said: / The reason on account of which I am angered, O god—hear that:
By self-restraint, purity, and severe penances, my body has been purified; / Indeed, ascetic practice for the span of a hundred thousand years was performed by me.
You see me thus, yet compassion does not arise from you in this way! / Therefore I am enraged this very day; I pronounce a curse thus!
Having heard this then from him, the wise one spoke to him. / Dharma said: / If I am destroyed, O highly intelligent one, the world will go to ruin.
Rooted in suffering, I, O dear one, severely emaciate [a person], O twice-born; / Afterwards I grant happiness, provided one does not abandon truth.
Sin is rooted in pleasure, but merit is obtained through hardship; / Performing merit in this way, a living being yields up life.

"In this way, I grant great happiness in the hereafter, no doubt."
Durvāsas said: "Happiness is obtained by one, but through that another experiences extreme misery.

For a mortal abandons it, and it is enjoyed by another.
Who understands that happiness? One does not see certainty at all.

I do not see that as good; what you do is indeed unjust.
By whichever body [an act] is performed, that happiness is not enjoyed [by it].

Affliction is performed by one, and it is also experienced by another.
Who understands that happiness, or whether it is injustice or righteousness?

Trouble is caused by one, and again happiness is enjoyed
by another person; if that is righteousness, all of it is combined with the highest good.

Merit also is performed by this one, and through this one experiences the fruit;
again, the merit that is being performed is enjoyed by another.

All that is indeed declared as happiness, which is such and possesses such characteristics.
And what is declared in the treatise on dharma is performed everywhere, not otherwise.

By whichever body they act, by that they endure suffering;
by that they enjoy in the hereafter, and likewise through this [body] too.
"Knowing this, may you, virtuous in soul, behold: / just as great-sinning thieves are struck together with their own bodies,"

harsh and severe through suffering, why is it not likewise with happiness?"
Dharma said: "By whichever body sinners perform their crime,

by that very [body] they indeed endure torment; for that is the fruit of crime.
A single punishment has been perceived as supreme in the treatises on dharma by the learned.

Know that [punishment] to be preceded by dharma, through these very principles, O king of dharma!"
Durvāsas said: "I do not accept such reasoning; listen likewise, O Dharmarāja!

Being enraged, I shall give you three curses; it will not be otherwise."
Dharma said: "When you are enraged, O greatly wise one, please forgive me!

If you do not forgive me, O king of brahmins, make me the son of a maidservant,
and you may make me a king, and a cāṇḍāla, O great sage!

A brahmin's face is always cheerful with grace toward one who bows."
And then Durvāsas, enraged, cursed Dharma:

Durvāsas said: "Become a king from dharma, and the son of a maidservant, not otherwise;
and go to the womb of a cāṇḍāla, O Dharma; go as you wish!"

Having thus given three curses, that best of brahmins departed.
Indeed, in this very connection, Dharma was seen in the past.

Somaśarman said: "What was Dharma like, having been cursed by that great soul?
Describe to me that form of his, if you know, O radiant woman!"

Sumanā said: "Dharma was born in the family of the Bharatas, having become Yudhiṣṭhira;
and he was Vidura, the son of a maidservant; and I shall mention the other one.

When King Hariścandra was tormented by Viśvāmitra,
then that highly intelligent Dharma attained the status of a cāṇḍāla.

Thus the fruit of action was experienced even by the great soul Dharma
from the curse of Durvāsas indeed; the truth has been spoken before you.

2.13.m:
Somaśarman said: "Tell me in detail the characteristic of celibacy;
and what kind of celibacy is it, if you know, O radiant woman?"

[Sumanā said:] "He whose delight is constantly in truth, a virtuous soul, would attain contentment;
when the fertile period has arrived, he may go to his own wife, free from fault.

He never abandons the virtuous conduct of his own family.
This alone is declared for the householder, O best of brahmins.

Celibacy for householders has indeed been described by me as supreme.
I shall explain that of ascetics; listen to it as I speak:

Endowed with self-restraint and truth, always afraid of sin,
having avoided intercourse with a woman, established in meditation and knowledge:

The celibacy of ascetics has thus been described before you.
I shall explain austerity itself; listen to it as I speak:

One should act with good conduct, free from desire and anger,
engaged in sustained effort for the benefit of living beings.

Austerity has thus been declared; I declare truth thus:
absence of greed toward others' possessions, and likewise toward others' wives;

he whose mind does not waver upon seeing them is called truthful.
I shall explain generosity, by which human beings live:

One who desires one's own happiness, whether here or in the hereafter,
[should know that] the great gift of food is indeed the giver of steady happiness.

Even a mere morsel should be given to one afflicted by hunger, without a doubt;
when it is given, great merit is gained, and he always enjoys nectar.

Day by day it should be given according to the capacity of one's wealth:
grass, a bed, words, and very cool shade of the house,

land, water, and likewise food, exceedingly pleasing speech,
a seat, conversation, devoid of deceit;

he who constantly does this for the sustenance of himself,
and who gives such a gift after worshipping the gods and ancestors,

rejoices here itself, and likewise in the hereafter.
He who, having become human, makes his day fruitful

through acts of giving and study, is a god, no doubt in this.
I shall also declare observance, the supreme means to dharma:

He who is devoted to the worship of the gods and the brahmins,
always endowed with observances, faithful in the vows of generosity, O one of good vows,

in benefactions and meritorious deeds—this is celebrated as observance.
I shall explain the nature of patience; let it be heard, O best of brahmins:

Having heard abuse by another, and when struck by someone,
one should not give way to anger, and struck, one should not strike back.

He should be forbearing; he is a virtuous soul, and he does not fall into passion;
he experiences supreme happiness both here and in the next world.

Thus patience has been declared; I declare purity thus:
He who is clean outside and inside, free from passion,

and behaves according to custom by bathing and sipping water—
thus purity has been declared; I shall explain non-violence:

Even a blade of grass should not be cut without purpose by a discerning person;
one should be devoted to non-violence toward others just as toward oneself.

I shall explain tranquility; through tranquility one enjoys happiness.
Tranquility alone should be cultivated; one should not abandon [virtue] out of distress.

Having cast off hostility toward creatures, one should train the mind in this manner.
Thus tranquility has been declared; I shall explain non-stealing:

Another's property must never be stolen, nor likewise another's wife;
with thought, words, and body one should so direct the mind.

I shall explain self-restraint before you, O best of brahmins:
by subduing the senses, and even the wavering mind,

one should destroy their insolence; then that conscious being is master [of himself].
I shall explain service, as it is in the treatises on dharma,

as it was declared by earlier teachers; I shall declare it thus:
With speech, body, and mind, one should accomplish the business of the guru.

That by which grace arises is spoken of as service.
Dharma with all its parts has been declared before you, O best of brahmins.

And I will tell you something else that you wish to hear, O husband:
Whatever man constantly abides in such dharma,

his rebirth does not occur again in the cycle of transmigration;
he goes to heaven through dharma: I speak the truth, the absolute truth."
Knowing this, O very wise one, follow dharma alone; / for everything that is [otherwise] unattainable on earth is obtained [through it], my beloved!
Through the grace of dharma, therefore, do heed my word! / Hearing his wife's word, the very wise Somaśarmā
spoke once again to that wife, Sumanā, who declared what is dharma.

2.14.m: Somaśarmā said: / How do you know such an auspicious, supreme exposition of dharma, O auspicious one? / And from whom was it heard by you?
Sumanā said: / Born in the lineage of the Bhārgavas, O high-minded one, was my father, / renowned by the name Cyavana, skilled in all knowledge.
I was his beloved daughter, dearer to him even than life. / Wherever he went, among sacred bathing sites and groves, O one of good vows,
and in assemblies of sages, and in shrines of deities, / I went with him alone, constantly playing.
Born in the lineage of Kuśika, the wise Vedaśarmā, / a friend of my father, arrived by chance while wandering about.
Overcome with great grief, thinking constantly [in sorrow], / my father said to that arrived great-souled one:
"I see that you are tormented with sorrow, O one of good vows; / why have you become sorrowful? Tell me the reason for that!"
Then, hearing these words of the great-souled Cyavana, / that one of good vows spoke to that great-souled father of mine:
"Vedaśarmā [am I], O very wise one; the cause of all my sorrow / is that my wife, highly virtuous and devoted to her husband,
has become childless, and my lineage does not continue. / This cause is declared to you, since I have been asked by you."
In the meantime, a certain Siddha arrived. / Standing up, by my father as well as by that Vedaśarmā,
that Siddha was worshipped by both of them with devotional offerings, / with gifts along with edible foods, and with words of sweet syllables.
The inner desire was asked by both, as was spoken earlier by you. / That righteous one addressed both of them—my father along with his friend:
"The entire cause of dharma has been declared to you by me indeed: / through dharma one obtains a son, wealth, grain, and wives."
Then, full dharma was performed by that Vedaśarmā; / from that dharma, great happiness arose, along with a son.
From the association with him, this firm conviction of mine arose, / which, my beloved, has been declared by me to you as supremely auspicious.
It was heard from that great Siddha, dispelling all doubt: / resorting to the dharma of a brāhmaṇa, follow it always!
Somaśarmā said: / Tell me what kind of death and what kind of birth occurs through dharma; / tell me all the characteristics of both, O beloved!
Sumanā said: / Through truth, purity, patience, tranquillity, and sacred bathing sites, merits, and so on, / by whoever dharma is protected, I shall describe his death:
Disease does not arise for him, nor pain in his body, / neither weariness nor languor, nor sweat, nor confusion.
Gandharvas and brāhmaṇas, having assumed divine forms, / endowed with the recitation of the Vedas, skilled in musical knowledge,
come to his side and sing peerless praise. / He is indeed at ease, seated on a seat, intent on worshipping the deity;
and the wise man, intent on dharma, attains a sacred place for bathing, / in the fire sanctuary, in a cowshed, and in shrines of deities,
in a pleasure grove, and at a pond where there is a sacred fig or banyan tree, / having taken recourse to a palāśa tree, and likewise to a bilva tree,
or having taken recourse to a stable for horses, or gone to a stable for elephants, / or when staying having taken recourse to an aśoka tree or a mango tree,
or in the presence of brāhmaṇas, or gone to a royal palace, / or having taken recourse to a battlefield where he might previously die.
Holy are the places of death, dharma alone being the cause; / having attained the rescue of cows, and likewise [the sacred place] Amarakaṇṭaka,
doing pure dharma continually, adhering to dharma, loving dharma, / he attains such a place when he meets death.
The best among men sees his virtuous mother and father, / his brother endowed with auspiciousness, and other relatives and kin,
being praised again and again by virtuous bards. / He does not at all see a sinful mother, father, or others.
Gandharvas sing songs, panegyrists praise with hymns, / and brāhmaṇas with the recitation of mantras; his mother honors him with affection,
and his father and circle of relatives [honor] the righteous, wise one. / Such are the messengers described, and such are your holy places, O lord.
He sees the messengers before his eyes, free of agitation, full of smiles and affection; / he [sees them] neither in sleep nor in delusion nor joined with distress.
The very wise Dharmarāja summons him: / "Come, come, O highly fortunate one, to where dharma abides!"
For him, no delusion, no wandering, no languor, no loss of memory / arises—there is no doubt of this; he remains with a serene soul.
Endowed with knowledge and discernment, remembering the god Janārdana, / he departs with them in this way, contented and joyful in mind.
A state of oneness arises there as he abandons his body; / taking recourse to the tenth door, his self departs.
A palanquin arrives for him, [or] a charming swan-vehicle, / or an aerial chariot arrives, or a horse, or an excellent elephant.
Being fanned all around with a held umbrella, / with chowries, and with fans by virtuous beings,
the righteous one is sung of and praised by learned men, / by bards, divine cāraṇas, and brāhmaṇas who have mastered the Vedas.
Praised by virtuous men and endowed with all happiness, / there he attains the fruit in accordance with the power of his gifts.
He travels happily through gardens and groves, / surrounded by divine apsarases, accompanied by auspicious things.
Praised by the gods, he beholds Dharmarāja, / and the gods endowed with dharma go out to meet him face to face:
"Come, come indeed, O highly fortunate one, enjoy pleasures pleasing to your mind!" / In this way he beholds Dharma of gentle form and great wisdom.
By the power of his own merit, he enjoys heaven itself; / when his pleasures are exhausted, that righteous one enters rebirth indeed.
Through the favor of his own dharma, he enters an auspicious family / of a highly virtuous brāhmaṇa, or likewise of a kṣatriya,
or of a highly virtuous, wealthy vaiśya, O wise one; / through dharma he rejoices there, and again performs merit.

2.15.m: Somaśarmā said: / With what kinds of characteristics is the death of sinners accompanied, O auspicious one? / Tell me that in detail, O fair lady, if you know it!
Sumanā said: / Listen, I shall explain what was heard by me from that Siddha, / as to what sign [appears] at the death of sinners, O beloved.
I shall tell of the place and the agony of great sinners: / a ground filled with feces, urine, and filth, accompanied by sins;
reaching that, that very wicked-souled one gives up his life-breaths with agony. / Having reached the ground of an outcaste, he goes to death in misery;
having resorted to ground frequented by donkeys or a courtesan's house, / or having gone to the house of a liquor-distiller, he approaches death.
Filled with bones, skin, and nails, enveloped by sins and crimes— / having reached such a place, that wicked-souled one certainly goes to death.
Having reached another ground of sinful conduct, he goes to death. / Now I will describe the movement of the messengers who desire [to seize] him:
formidable, harsh, frightful, extremely black, with huge bellies, / with tawny eyes, yellow and blue, extremely white, with huge bellies,
very tall, terrifying, looking like dried flesh and fat, / with fierce fangs, formidable, with lion-faces and serpents in their hands.
Seeing them, he trembles and grieves again and again. / Terrible loud roars like the howling of jackals, O highly intelligent one,
all the messengers release at the base of his ears. / Binding him at the throat with nooses, and binding his waist and belly,
overpowering him, they cast him down; he cries out repeatedly, 'Alas, alas!' / I shall declare the agony of the one dying, just as it is.
The theft of another's wealth, the violation of another's wife, / a debt, the entire property of another seized by sinners,
which was never returned due to delusion caused by greed for pleasure, / and likewise other great sins, and even improper acceptance of gifts—
all these rise up into the throat of that dying man. / And whatever sins were previously committed,
they come to the base of his throat, of that great sinner, not otherwise; / they generate severe agony through the obstruction of phlegm.
With severe pains his throat rattles; / he weeps, trembles excessively, and repeatedly [recalls] his mother and father,
he remembers his brother there, and his wife and sons again and again; / again he enters forgetfulness, bewildered by great sin.
His life-breaths depart, agitated by abundant pain; / he falls, and he trembles, and he faints again and again.
Thus afflicted with agony, he experiences misery, utterly bewildered. / His life-breaths, stirred with great difficulty by severe distress,
depart through the downward passage, hear, O beloved! / Thus the living being, deeply deluded, endowed with greed and confusion,
is led away by Yama's messengers; I will tell of his misery.

2.16.m: Sumanā said: / He is led along a path strewn with burning coals, dragged along; / burning, that wicked-souled one struggles again and again,
where the heat is very fierce, heated as if by twelve suns; / he is led by that path, scorched by the rays of the sun,
over impassable mountains that are devoid of shade, the evil-minded one; / he is led by that path, afflicted with hunger and thirst.
Struck by the messengers with clubs, swords, and axes, / and beaten with whips, reviled by the messengers,
then on an icy path he is blown upon by the wind again; / through that cold, becoming miserable, he proceeds, without a doubt.
Being dragged by the messengers, he is led through diverse impassable places; / thus the sinner, that wicked-souled reviler of gods and Brahmins,
who engaged in all manner of sins, is led by Yama's servants. / The wicked-souled one beholds Yama, resembling a mass of black collyrium,
fierce, terrible, dreadful, surrounded by dreadful messengers, / encompassed by all diseases, accompanied by Citragupta,
mounted upon a buffalo, the god Dharmarāja, O best of Brahmins, / with terrifying fangs, very fierce, his mouth resembling death itself,
wearing yellow garments, club in hand, anointed with red fragrant paste, / adorned with red garlands, mace in hand, terrifying.
The evil-minded one beholds Yama of such form, huge in body; / seeing him arrived, excluded from all dharma,
Yama beholds that wicked, most sinful thorn of dharma; / he punishes him with great miseries, with torments, and with wooden mallets.
He is cooked for as long a time as the end of a thousand yugas; / and in various kinds of hell he is cooked again and again.
The evildoer goes to a hellish womb among crores of worms; / he is constantly cooked in filth, crying 'Alas, alas!', devoid of consciousness.
And thus that sinful-souled one certainly goes to death; / thus the evil-minded one experiences the consequence of his sin.
I will tell of his rebirth, and in which wombs he goes: / having obtained a hundred wombs of dogs, he experiences the sin again;
the wicked-souled one becomes a tiger, and again goes to the womb of a female ass, / to the womb of a cat, a sow, and likewise to the womb of a snake,
among all the different varieties of beasts again and again; / he enters into sinful birds, and into other large creatures;
the evildoer goes to the womb of an outcaste, of a Bhilla, and of a Pulinda woman. / All this has been declared to you, both the birth of sinners
and, hear, O beloved, their very terrible agony at death. / The conduct of sin and merit has been narrated before you by me;
I shall speak of another matter thus, if you ask, O honor-giver.
